 Photo by Vladimir Srajber 
 🛒 Disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Quick Answer: The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the best all-round RV power station for 2026, with 4,000W continuous output and 4,096Wh of capacity. If you mainly run a roof air conditioner on weekend trips, the Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro is simpler. Budget shoppers should look at the BLUETTI AC200L and its built-in 30A RV outlet.
 Table of Contents 
 RV season in Ontario runs from the May long weekend to Thanksgiving, and the electrical pedestals at most provincial parks top out at 30 amps. That is enough for lights, a fridge and a laptop charger. Add a roof air conditioner or an induction cooktop and the pedestal breaker trips. A portable power station fills that gap, and unlike a gas generator it can run inside the coach or under the awning with no exhaust at all. If you already own a small unit for tailgates, our portable power station guide explains where those compact models stop being useful. This comparison covers five units that hold up under real trailer loads.
 The picks below were sorted on four measured numbers: continuous AC output, surge output, usable capacity and charge time. Real campsite loads matter far more than the number on the box. A 13,500 BTU roof air conditioner draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W on compressor startup, so a station rated at 1,000W will not get it off the line no matter what the marketing claims. Runtime figures here are calculated at 85 percent inverter efficiency, which is where most lithium units land under a steady 500W load. There is a second use case worth naming. Outage statistics show that the same battery you carry in the trailer can keep a furnace fan and fridge alive at home during a winter storm.
 Safety rules do not soften because the power source is smaller. RV shore inlets, transfer switches and any permanent wiring in a trailer fall under Ontario electrical rules, and the Electrical Safety Authority requires a licensed electrician for anything beyond plugging into an existing outlet. Carbon monoxide is the other hard line. Battery stations produce none, which is why one can sit on the dinette table, but a gas generator stays outside and away from windows and vents. The CSA Group publishes the standards behind both the appliances and the CO alarms you should have on board, and our generator safety guide covers placement distances in detail.
 Choosing comes down to three questions. How many watts does your largest single load need at startup? How many hours do you need it to run? How much weight can you lift into a storage bay? A 2,000Wh station weighs between 40 and 55 pounds, which one person can handle. Anything above 3,000Wh usually means two people or a dedicated cart. Solar input matters as well, since most Ontario parks enforce quiet hours and a 300W to 400W folding array will refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun. Buy for the load you actually run, not the one you imagine running.

 1. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 , Best for Full-Time Boondocking # 
 Photo via Pexels 
 EcoFlow’s flagship tops this list because it comes closest to a 30A campsite pedestal in battery form. Continuous output is rated at 4,000W with an 8,000W surge, and capacity starts at 4,096Wh. Add expansion batteries and the total passes 12kWh, which is more than most travel trailers burn through in a long weekend. A 13,500 BTU roof air conditioner pulls about 1,500W running, so one battery holds it for roughly 2.3 hours at 85 percent inverter efficiency. Swap the air conditioner for a 12V compressor fridge, LED lighting, a laptop and a Starlink dish, and the same battery runs two full days. The EcoFlow product page lists both 120V and 240V output modes, so the unit can also feed a home transfer switch between camping trips.
 Noise is where it walks away from a gas generator. EcoFlow rates fan noise under 30 dBA at low load, quieter than the refrigerator in your kitchen. A 2,200W inverter generator sitting outside the same trailer runs 52 to 57 dBA at 23 feet, and it cannot legally run during quiet hours at most Ontario parks. Recharge speed is the second headline number: 0 to 80 percent in about 50 minutes from a 120V wall outlet with the AC charging cable.
 Two honest complaints. The unit is heavy, heavy enough that lifting it into a truck bed or a high storage bay is a two-person job. App-first controls also add steps when you just want to press a button and go. Pair it with a standard TT-30 dogbone adapter to feed the trailer’s shore power inlet. Check the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 on Amazon .
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ Headroom that matches a 30A campsite pedestal: 4,000W continuous and 8,000W surge.
 ✅ Expandable capacity from 4,096Wh to more than 12kWh with add-on batteries.
 ✅ Quiet enough for park quiet hours at under 30 dBA under light load.
 ✅ Fast AC recharge, roughly 0 to 80 percent in 50 minutes.
 ✅ Doubles as home backup through a transfer switch between camping seasons.
 ❌ Heavy enough that moving it is a two-person job.
 ❌ The most expensive option here once expansion batteries are added.
 ❌ App-first controls frustrate people who want a simple on button.
 Who it’s for: Full-time RVers and boondockers who run air conditioning off-grid and want one battery that also backs up the house.
 2. Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro , Best for Running RV Air Conditioning # 
 Jackery built this one for the exact load that trips a 15A campsite breaker. The Explorer 3000 Pro delivers 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge from a 3,024Wh pack, which is enough headroom to start a 13,500 BTU air conditioner without bolting on a soft-start kit. Run the numbers on paper: at 85 percent efficiency the pack holds about 2,570 usable watt hours, so a 1,500W air conditioner runs for roughly 1.7 hours and a 300W fridge-plus-fan load runs for about 8.5 hours. On a July weekend in Killarney, that is the difference between sleeping comfortably and sleeping in a hot trailer.
 Operation is simple by design. Large physical buttons, a clear display and a phone app if you want it. Jackery also sells a matching transfer switch, so the same station can carry a furnace fan and refrigerator at home during a winter outage. Working out your own numbers takes ten minutes with the label on the appliance, and our refrigerator runtime guide walks through the arithmetic step by step.
 The catch is recharging. A full AC charge takes about two hours, but 1,400W of solar is an enormous amount of panel to carry and store, and Ontario shoulder-season sun rarely delivers rated output for a full day. There is also no 30A RV outlet on the front panel, so a dogbone adapter is mandatory. Check the Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro on Amazon .
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ 3,000W continuous and 6,000W surge, enough to start a roof air conditioner.
 ✅ Simple physical controls with a readable display and no mandatory app.
 ✅ About a two-hour AC recharge at this capacity class.
 ✅ A matching transfer switch is available for home backup duty.
 ❌ No 30A RV outlet on the front panel, so a dogbone adapter is required.
 ❌ Reaching 1,400W of solar charging means carrying a large panel array.
 ❌ Close to 64 pounds, which is awkward to move alone.
 Who it’s for: Weekend and seasonal campers who want to run a roof air conditioner on battery power without learning a complicated app.
 3. BLUETTI AC200L , Best Mid-Range Value # 
 The AC200L is the value pick because it puts a dedicated 30A RV outlet on the front panel at a fraction of flagship capacity. Output is 2,400W continuous with 3,600W of surge in Power Lifting mode, and the LiFePO4 pack holds 2,048Wh. That works out to roughly 1,740 usable watt hours at 85 percent efficiency. A 900W induction cooktop runs for about 1.9 hours on a single charge, and a 60W CPAP machine runs close to 29 nights. For a trailer with a 30A shore inlet, no dogbone adapter is needed, which removes one more part to lose in a storage bin.
 Charging is quick for the class. BLUETTI rates 0 to 80 percent in about 45 minutes from a wall outlet, and the unit accepts a folding solar array directly with no separate charge controller. Fans are audible at full output, roughly in the 50 dBA range, but that still sits well below any gas generator and the noise fades as the load drops.
 Two limits matter. There is no 240V output, so this is not a home backup unit in the way the DELTA Pro 3 is. Capacity also fills up fast once an air conditioner is running, and each expansion battery adds significant cost. Check the BLUETTI AC200L on Amazon .
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ Dedicated 30A RV outlet built into the front panel.
 ✅ 2,400W continuous with 3,600W of surge in Power Lifting mode.
 ✅ Fast recharge, about 0 to 80 percent in 45 minutes on AC.
 ✅ LiFePO4 cells with a long cycle life and good cold-weather behaviour.
 ❌ No 240V output, so it cannot feed a home transfer switch the way larger units can.
 ❌ 2,048Wh drains quickly with an air conditioner running.
 ❌ Fan noise is noticeable at full output.
 Who it’s for: Trailer owners who want a genuine 30A RV outlet and fast charging without paying flagship prices.
 4. Anker SOLIX F2600 , Best for High-Surge Loads # 
 Photo via Pexels 
 Anker’s SOLIX F2600 targets trailers that draw hard for short bursts. The rating is 2,400W continuous and 3,600W surge from a 2,560Wh LiFePO4 pack, and the front panel includes an RV-style 30A outlet plus USB-C ports rated at 100W and 140W. Surge headroom is the selling point for anyone running a coffee maker, a hair dryer or a microwave alongside the fridge. Anker also rates AC recharge at roughly 1.5 hours, which is quicker than most competitors at this capacity.
 Weight lands just under 70 pounds, so it wants a permanent home in the trailer rather than a spot on the picnic table. Build quality is the strongest part of the package: steel-reinforced corners, a proper carry handle and a five-year warranty that matches the better units in this comparison. For a couple who mostly stays on electrical sites and wants insurance against a tripped pedestal breaker, that combination is hard to argue with.
 The compromises are capacity and solar. At 2,560Wh it sits between the budget and flagship tiers, so an air conditioner on a hot afternoon will drain it in under two hours. Solar input is also lower than the EcoFlow and Jackery flagships, which matters if you camp off-grid for more than two nights at a time.
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ 3,600W surge from a 2,400W continuous rating handles motor starts.
 ✅ RV-style 30A outlet plus 100W and 140W USB-C ports on the panel.
 ✅ AC recharge in about 1.5 hours, among the fastest in this class.
 ✅ Steel-reinforced build with a five-year warranty.
 ❌ Just under 70 pounds, so it stays where you put it.
 ❌ 2,560Wh is mid-tier capacity for the asking price.
 ❌ Solar input is lower than the EcoFlow and Jackery flagships.
 Who it’s for: RV owners who run high-surge appliances in short bursts and want a rugged station that can also sit in a garage for home backup.
 5. Goal Zero Yeti 1500X , Best Compact Solar-First Setup # 
 The Yeti 1500X is the light option in this group. At roughly 44 pounds it is the only station here that one person can move from a truck bed to a dinette without help, and the 1,516Wh pack still delivers 2,000W continuous and 3,500W surge. That surge rating will start a 13,500 BTU air conditioner if you fit a soft-start kit to the unit. Without the kit, expect the overload light and a shutdown. Honest numbers: 1,516Wh is about 1,290 usable watt hours, so a 60W fridge load runs roughly 21 hours and a 500W load runs about 2.5 hours.
 Where the Yeti earns its place is solar. Goal Zero’s MPPT charging and the Yeti Link expansion system suit campers who want to build capacity over a few seasons rather than buy it all at once. A 300W folding panel refills the pack in roughly six hours of good summer sun, which fits a typical park day. Our solar panel guide for camping covers which folding arrays pair well with packs at this size, and the solar generator comparison explains how MPPT charging differs between brands.
 Caveats are straightforward. This is a smaller pack, so it will not run a trailer’s air conditioning through a warm night. DC car charging is slow, and the included wall charger is not the fastest way to top up between trips.
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ About 44 pounds, the lightest unit in this comparison.
 ✅ 2,000W continuous and 3,500W surge from a 1,516Wh pack.
 ✅ MPPT solar charging that pairs well with a 300W folding panel.
 ✅ Expandable over time through the Yeti Link system.
 ❌ Needs a soft-start kit to run a 13,500 BTU air conditioner.
 ❌ Smaller pack, so overnight air conditioning is out of reach.
 ❌ Slow DC charging from a vehicle 12V outlet.
 Who it’s for: Solo travellers and small-trailer owners who prioritize low weight and quiet solar charging over raw capacity.
 Frequently Asked Questions # 
 How many watts do I need to run an RV air conditioner? 
 A 13,500 BTU roof unit draws about 1,500W running and can spike past 3,000W on compressor startup. Look for a station rated at 2,000W continuous and 3,500W surge or better, or fit a soft-start kit to cut the startup spike.
 Can I run a power station inside an RV? 
 Yes. Battery stations produce no exhaust, so they can sit on the dinette or floor while running. Keep the vents and fans clear, and never run a gas generator inside a trailer or under an attached awning.
 How long will a 2,000Wh station run a 12V RV fridge? 
 A modern 12V compressor fridge averages 40 to 60W once it is cold. At 85 percent inverter efficiency, 2,048Wh works out to roughly 29 to 43 hours, depending on ambient temperature and how often the door opens.
 Do I need an electrician to connect a power station to my RV? 
 Not for plugging into the existing shore power inlet with an adapter. Any hardwired transfer switch, new outlet or panel work falls under Ontario electrical rules, and the Electrical Safety Authority expects a licensed electrician to do it.
 Will a power station charge while I drive? 
 Most units accept 100W to 200W through a 12V car port, so a four-hour drive adds a few hundred watt hours. A dedicated DC-to-DC charger feeds more power, but it needs proper wiring and a fuse.
 Are solar panels worth adding for Ontario camping? 
 Yes, if you camp off-grid. A 300W to 400W folding array refills a mid-size station in one decent summer day. Expect noticeably less in May and late September when the sun sits lower in the sky.
 What Should You Remember? # 
 Match surge, not just running watts. A 13,500 BTU air conditioner needs 2,000W continuous and 3,500W surge or better.
 Plan for 85 percent efficiency. A 2,000Wh pack delivers roughly 1,700 usable watt hours under a steady load.
 Weight decides placement. Units above 60 pounds stay in the trailer, while lighter packs move to the picnic table.
 Quiet hours favor batteries. No gas generator can legally run overnight in most Ontario parks.
 Check the outlet type. A built-in 30A RV port removes the need for a dogbone adapter at the shore inlet.
 Battery stations make no carbon monoxide. That is why they are safe inside a trailer, unlike a gasoline generator.
 Bring solar if you boondock. A 300W folding array refills a mid-size pack in one summer day.
 This article is for general information only. Always follow manufacturer instructions, local electrical codes, and hire a licensed electrician for transfer switches and standby generator installation. Carbon monoxide is deadly , never run a generator indoors.

 What Makes a Portable Power Station Good for an RV?

 The Battery Must Match Your Daily Energy Requirement 
 Capacity in watt-hours determines how much energy the station stores.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh per day

 That does not mean the 4kWh model is automatically better.

 The lesson is:
 TT-30 present ≠ full 30A shore-service capability 
 Read the exact port limit.
 12V and High-Amp DC Matter in an RV 
 An RV contains many DC loads.
 Converting:
 battery DC → inverter AC → RV converter DC 
 can be less direct than supplying compatible DC equipment from a regulated DC output.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 includes a 30A Anderson DC output rated at 378W total alongside additional DC connections.
 The BLUETTI AC200L includes a 48V/8A regulated RV output as well as a conventional 12V/10A car socket. BLUETTI also offers its D40 voltage-regulator accessory for RV DC applications.
 Those features can matter more for serious RV use than another USB outlet.
 Solar Input Determines How Quickly You Can Recover Off Grid 
 A larger battery is useful only if you can replenish it.
 Current manufacturer limits among our recommendations range from around:
 1,000W to 3,200W maximum solar input 
 depending on the exact model and configuration.
 Do not treat the maximum input number as expected all-day production.
 Solar output changes with sunlight, shading, panel angle, temperature, array configuration, and the station’s electrical limits.
 Alternator Charging Can Be Critical for RV Travel 
 A motorhome or tow vehicle may spend hours driving between campsites.
 That makes the alternator a potentially valuable charging source.
 EcoFlow currently offers an 800W Alternator Charger compatible with the DELTA Pro 3 when the required cable/adapter arrangement is used.  These are optional charging systems, not justification for connecting arbitrary high-current loads directly to a vehicle electrical system.
 Expansion Matters More for RVs Than for Short Camping Trips 
 Your RV power requirement can grow.
 An initial system might only supply:

 Later, you may add:

 Starlink;

 air conditioning;
 electric cooking;

 A station that accepts expansion batteries can grow without replacing the inverter unit.
 Expansion therefore carries substantial weight in this ranking.

 campground shore power → driving → boondocking → solar charging

 Choose the Apex 300 if you want an RV power platform that can grow substantially over time rather than a fixed-capacity portable station.

 It can also supply 120/240V through its high-power connection architecture.
 For an RV system with substantial electrical loads, that can be more useful than an extra few hundred watt-hours of battery capacity.
 Solar input is also excellent at up to 3,200W on the F3800 Plus generation.

 Do not assume the TT-30 port can deliver the full 6,000W inverter capability.

 For a normal 30A RV that only uses TT-30, this makes the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus a cleaner match to full 3,600W theoretical 30A service.

 At 136.7 pounds, this is not a casually portable battery.
 It has wheels, but getting it up RV steps, into a pickup bed, or through a tight storage compartment can still require planning or more than one person.
 Its high-output capability is also unnecessary if your RV loads peak at only 1,500W.
 An independent 2026 field review praised the F3800 Plus’s power and expansion but similarly penalized portability because of its size and weight.

 you want a very large expansion ceiling;

 High for specifications; Medium-High for RV-specific field evidence. 
 Current Anker documentation clearly defines the exact F3800 Plus generation and its port limits, avoiding confusion with the older F3800.
 Which Portable Power Station Is Best for a 30-Amp RV? 
 For a straightforward 30A RV connection, our first choice is the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus .
 Its TT-30 output is rated:
 120V × 30A = 3,600W 
 which matches the theoretical maximum of conventional 30A RV shore power.
 That does not mean you should intentionally operate at the limit continuously.
 You still need to account for:
 startup demand;
 battery runtime;
 converter load;
 simultaneous appliances;
 manufacturer limits.
 The other TT-30 models remain useful but differ in available output:
 BLUETTI AC200L: 2,400W total inverter
 Anker F3800 Plus TT-30: 3,000W maximum
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus TT-30: 3,600W maximum
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: 4,000W total system output in its applicable 120V mode
 This is why comparing the plug alone is misleading.
 Which Portable Power Station Is Best for a 50-Amp RV? 
 A normal 50A campground connection can theoretically provide:
 120V × 50A × 2 legs = 12,000W 
 None of the single power stations on this page should be described as a complete 12kW replacement for unrestricted 50A campground shore service.
 Instead, identify the loads you actually need.
 The most relevant single-unit candidates for higher-power RV systems are:
 Anker F3800 Plus for 6,000W 120/240V output
 and:
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 for 4,000W 120/240V capability.
 The BLUETTI Apex 300 also provides a more advanced modular architecture that can expand into larger multi-unit systems.
 A 50A RV owner should therefore think in terms of:
 load-managed backup/off-grid power 
 rather than:
 full campground service replacement 
 unless the exact multi-unit system has been designed and verified to provide the required electrical architecture.
 Which Is Best for RV Air Conditioning? 
 Air conditioning requires two separate qualifications:
 Can the station start and run the air conditioner? 
 and:
 Does it contain enough energy to run it for the required time? 
 A 6,000W inverter does not automatically mean long air-conditioner runtime.
 Suppose an exact RV air conditioner averages, hypothetically:
 1,300W 
 for four hours.
 Energy requirement:
 1,300 × 4 = 5,200Wh 
 before other RV loads and conversion losses.
 That already exceeds the base capacity of every station on this page.
 For longer A/C runtime, expansion batteries and recharge capability become more important than maximum inverter wattage alone.
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3, Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus, BLUETTI Apex 300, and Anker F3800 Plus are therefore stronger air-conditioning platforms than a fixed 2kWh battery because they can grow into multi-kWh systems.
 The exact A/C startup and running requirements still need to be checked.
 Which Is Best for RV Solar? 
 For maximum published direct solar-input capability among the products here:
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus — up to 3,200W 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 — up to 2,600W 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 — up to 2,400W 
 BLUETTI AC200L — up to 1,200W 
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus — up to 1,000W 
 However, maximum PV input is not enough to choose a system.
 You also need:
 compatible panel voltage;
 array open-circuit voltage;
 current limits;
 connector architecture;
 roof area;
 shading;
 realistic solar harvest.
 See How to Charge a Portable Power Station With Solar Panels before connecting an RV solar array.
 Which Is Best for Charging While Driving? 
 Among these picks, EcoFlow currently has the clearest high-power vehicle-charging path.
 Its 800W Alternator Charger supports the DELTA Pro 3 when used with the required custom connection hardware. EcoFlow states that it can add approximately 1kWh in 1.3 hours under its specified conditions.
 BLUETTI’s current AC200L ecosystem also supports an optional 560W alternator charger.
 A hypothetical energy comparison illustrates why this matters.
 At:
 800W × 3 hours driving = 2,400Wh idealized input 
 versus:
 100W × 3 hours = 300Wh 
 a high-power DC-DC charging system can fundamentally change how much base battery capacity an RV needs.
 Real charging power may be lower, and vehicle alternator capability must be verified.
 Is a 2kWh or 4kWh Power Station Better for an RV? 
 A 2kWh station is usually more attractive when:
 daily loads are modest;
 solar is reliable;
 the station must be moved;
 air conditioning is not a major battery load;
 the RV already has a house battery.
 That is where the BLUETTI AC200L fits.
 A 3–4kWh station is more attractive when:
 daily energy use exceeds roughly 1kWh;
 recharging is uncertain;
 you want meaningful overnight reserve;
 appliances use more AC power;
 expansion is likely.
 That is where the:
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 and:
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 become stronger choices.
 How Expansion Changes the Recommendation 
 Base capacity is only the beginning for most products here.
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 A base unit contains:
 3,584Wh 
 One HomePower 3600 Plus can support five compatible expansion batteries for approximately:
 21.5kWh total 
 according to Jackery.
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 Base:
 4,096Wh 
 One unit can expand to roughly:
 12kWh 
 using two DELTA Pro 3 extra batteries. Larger multi-unit EcoFlow systems can scale substantially further.
 BLUETTI AC200L 
 Base:
 2,048Wh 
 BLUETTI’s current U.S. configuration supports expansion beyond:
 7.5kWh 
 depending on compatible battery selection.
 BLUETTI Apex 300 
 Base:
 2,764.8Wh 
 The Apex platform is designed around extensive B300-family expansion and multi-unit architecture, with BLUETTI advertising system configurations reaching approximately 58kWh.
 Anker F3800 Plus 
 Base:
 3,840Wh 
 With six 3,840Wh BP3800 expansion batteries:
 3.84kWh × 7 total battery modules = 26.88kWh 
 for one expanded inverter system.
 Larger paired configurations can scale further.
 Do not buy expansion capacity you do not need.
 A modular ceiling is valuable because it gives you a path forward—not because the largest possible configuration is automatically the correct one.
 Weight Matters Inside an RV 
 Battery weight can affect more than convenience.
 Our recommendations range from roughly:
 62 pounds 
 to:
 137 pounds 
 before expansion batteries.
 Model 
 Approximate base weight 
 BLUETTI AC200L 
 62.4 lb 
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus 
 77.2 lb 
 BLUETTI Apex 300 
 83.8 lb 
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 
 113.5 lb 
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus 
 136.7 lb 
 That weight needs to be:
 physically accommodated;
 safely secured during travel;
 considered against RV cargo limits;
 placed where ventilation remains adequate.
 Expansion batteries add more weight.
 The best RV battery system is not one that creates a payload or storage problem.
 Don’t Ignore the RV Converter 
 If you connect the portable power station to the RV’s shore-power inlet, the RV converter/charger may activate.
 That can make the energy path:
 PPS battery → AC inverter → RV converter → RV 12V system / house battery 
 The converter itself may therefore become part of the load.
 This is one reason direct DC capability can be useful.
 It is also why a station connected to an RV inlet can consume energy faster than a simple list of visible 120V appliances suggests.
 For the full architecture discussion, return to What Size Portable Power Station Do You Need for an RV? .
 Portable Power Station vs RV House Battery 
 A portable power station and an RV house battery system are not automatically interchangeable.
 A conventional RV system may integrate:
 house battery;
 converter/charger;
 inverter;
 DC distribution;
 AC distribution;
 shore power;
 solar controller;
 alternator charger.
 A portable station packages many related functions into one device, but the electrical architecture is different.
 The right role may be:
 supplement 
 rather than:
 replace. 
 Products such as the AC200L, Apex 300 and DELTA Pro 3 include increasingly sophisticated RV/DC features, but permanent integration should still follow the exact manufacturers’ supported configuration.
 Safety and Connection Considerations 
 Do not connect a portable power station to an RV with improvised backfeeding or homemade high-current wiring.
 Before feeding the RV shore inlet, verify:
 output voltage;
 outlet limit;
 adapter rating;
 RV inlet type;
 neutral-ground behavior;
 electrical management system compatibility;
 simultaneous load.
 A physically compatible plug does not guarantee complete electrical compatibility.
 Large power stations also need to be secured during travel.
 Do not allow a 60–140 pound battery to move freely inside the RV.
 Keep cooling openings clear, follow the exact manufacturer temperature limits, and do not assume that an outdoor/RV product is waterproof.
 See the Portable Power Station Safety Guide for broader ownership guidance.
 Recall and Current-Market Check 
 Power Station Scout searched the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recall database for the exact recommended model names during the September 11, 2026 evidence review.
 No exact-model recall notice surfaced in our searches for:
 Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus;
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3;
 BLUETTI AC200L;
 BLUETTI Apex 300;
 Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus.
 That is a dated search result—not a guarantee that a model has never been recalled or will not be recalled later.
 CPSC states that its online recall data is updated as new recalls and product-safety warnings are announced.
 Exact-model recall status should therefore be checked again immediately before publication and during future commercial updates.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What is the best portable power station for an RV? 
 For a typical 30A RV, our best overall choice is the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus because it combines 3,584Wh capacity, a 3,600W inverter, native TT-30, major battery expansion, and a comparatively manageable 77-pound chassis.
 For a more advanced off-grid system with strong solar, DC and alternator capabilities, we prefer the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 .
 What is the best portable power station for a 30-amp RV? 
 The Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our strongest direct 30A match because Jackery rates its TT-30 outlet at 120V/30A and its inverter at 3,600W.
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lighter alternative if your actual loads remain under 2,400W.
 What is the best portable power station for a 50-amp RV? 
 A 50A RV can theoretically access far more power from campground service than any single recommendation here supplies.
 For high-output load-managed use, look first at the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus or EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 because both support 120/240V architectures.
 Do not assume either recreates unrestricted 12kW campground 50A service.
 Is 2,000Wh enough for an RV? 
 It can be.
 A 2kWh station is useful when your RV loads are modest or when daily solar and vehicle charging replace much of the energy used.
 It may be insufficient for extended air conditioning, heavy electric cooking, or multiple days without charging.
 Is 3,600Wh enough for an RV? 
 For many moderate RV energy budgets, 3.5–4kWh is a substantial amount of storage.
 If your RV consumes:
 1,200Wh/day 
 a 3,584Wh rated battery represents roughly three days of headline capacity before losses and reserve.
 If the RV consumes:
 5,000Wh/day 
 the same battery is less than one day’s requirement.
 Which RV power station has the most solar input here? 
 The Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus has the largest manufacturer-specified solar-input ceiling among our five main recommendations at up to 3,200W .
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 follows at 2,600W .
 Which is the lightest RV power station in this list? 
 The BLUETTI AC200L is the lightest at approximately 62.4 pounds .
 It also has the smallest base battery among our five recommendations at 2,048Wh.
 Which RV power station is best for alternator charging? 
 The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 currently has the strongest clearly documented first-party vehicle-charging ecosystem among these picks through EcoFlow’s 800W Alternator Charger.
 BLUETTI offers an optional 560W alternator charger for the AC200L.
 Can I plug my RV directly into one of these power stations? 
 Some have native TT-30 outputs designed for this purpose.
 That still requires you to verify:
 the RV load;
 station output limit;
 grounding behavior;
 converter load;
 RV electrical-management system;
 manufacturer instructions.
 Do not treat physical plug compatibility as complete system compatibility.
 Can these run an RV air conditioner? 
 Some can, depending on the exact air conditioner.
 Continuous output and startup demand must both qualify.
 Runtime then depends on the battery capacity and how long the compressor operates.
 An air conditioner can consume several kilowatt-hours during extended use, so expansion and recharging often become central to the system.
 Do I need a TT-30 outlet? 
 Not necessarily.
 You can power individual RV appliances directly from ordinary AC, USB or DC outputs.
 A TT-30 is especially useful when you want a straightforward physical connection to a 30A RV shore-power inlet.
 Is 240V useful in an RV power station? 
 Only if your actual RV electrical architecture or loads require it.
 Most conventional 30A RVs use 120V.
 Larger 50A RVs use a split-phase service architecture, but a portable power station’s 240V capability does not automatically reproduce full 50A campground service.
 Bottom Line 
 For a typical 30A RV , the Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus is our best overall portable power station .
 Its combination of:
 3,584Wh battery + 3,600W AC output + native 30A TT-30 + expansion to roughly 21.5kWh + 77-pound chassis 
 creates the strongest balance of RV electrical fit, stored energy, scalability, and transportability.
 Choose the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 when you need a more capable off-grid ecosystem with 4,096Wh of base capacity, 2,600W solar input, high-amp DC, alternator charging, and sophisticated 120/240V options.
 Choose the BLUETTI AC200L when a 2kWh battery is enough and you want TT-30, RV-oriented DC outputs, expansion, strong solar input, and much less base weight.
 Choose the BLUETTI Apex 300 when you want to build a modular RV energy platform rather than simply buy one fixed portable power station.
 Choose the Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus when high continuous output and 120/240V capability outweigh the considerable size and weight.
 But the product comes after the requirement.
 The correct decision sequence remains:
 RV loads → connection method → simultaneous watts → startup watts → daily Wh → recharge plan → required capacity → qualified models 
 If you do not yet know those requirements, begin with What Size Portable Power Station Do You Need for an RV? .

 Coverage status
This guide reflects published specifications, manufacturer data, and category-wide research as of the publication date. Our in-house bench testing for individual units is ongoing. Full hands-on findings (real-world capacity, recharge timing, noise) will be added in updates marked clearly above.

 How we ranked these
 RV power station selection depends on five factors, in priority order:
 TT-30 or NEMA 14-50 outlet built in. Direct RV shore-power hookup eliminates adapter friction.
 Rooftop AC startup capacity. 13.5K BTU units need 2,300-2,700 W surge; 15K BTU units need 2,500-3,000 W. Soft-start kits reduce this by 50-65%.
 Solar input ceiling. For boondocking, the unit must accept enough solar input to keep up with daytime appliance draw.
 240 V split-phase support. Only required for 50 A RV setups (fifth-wheels, Class A). Anker SOLIX F3800 is the single-unit answer; EcoFlow Delta Pro requires paired units plus the Double Voltage Hub.
 Weight and storage footprint. RV storage bays are constrained; lighter and smaller wins for solo loading.

 Frequently asked questions
 FAQ Best Portable Power Station for RV FAQ 
 Can any of these run a 13.5K BTU rooftop AC? 
 + The Bluetti AC200L, EcoFlow Delta 2 Max, and Anker SOLIX F3800 all reliably start 13.5K BTU rooftop AC. The DJI Power 1000 V2 can start it with a soft-start kit installed; without one, it's marginal. The smaller units (Bluetti AC180, Jackery Explorer 1000 v2) cannot reliably start a 13.5K BTU AC without a soft-start kit reducing the surge demand.
 What's the difference between a TT-30 and a 14-50 outlet? 
 + TT-30 is the standard 30 A RV shore-power connector (single 120 V circuit). NEMA 14-50 is the 50 A RV connector for big rigs (240 V split-phase, two 120 V circuits). Bluetti AC200L and EcoFlow Delta 2 Max have built-in TT-30 outlets (work with 30 A RVs). Anker SOLIX F3800 has a NEMA 14-50 outlet (works with 50 A RVs). For mismatched setups, use a 30A-to-50A or 50A-to-30A dogbone adapter (~$30).
 How much solar input do I actually need for boondocking? 
 + Plan for solar wattage equal to your average hourly draw, times 4-5 (to account for non-peak-sun hours and cloud coverage). For a typical RV draw of 100-200 W average (fridge + lights + electronics), 400-1,000 W of solar covers daily use indefinitely. For RVs running AC during the day, plan 1,200-2,000 W of solar minimum.
 Do I need a transfer switch to connect a power station to my RV? 
 + No, not for portable use. Plug the power station into your RV's shore power inlet directly via TT-30 or 14-50 cord. The RV's existing 12 V converter, fridge, lights, and outlets all work as if you were plugged into campground shore power. For permanent installation with automatic switching (battery banks integrated into the RV), an inverter/charger with built-in transfer switch (Victron MultiPlus or similar) is the right tool — not a portable power station.
 Can I charge a power station from my RV's truck while driving? 
 + Yes, via 12 V cigarette port (slow — most stations accept 8-10 A from 12 V, taking 12-24 hours for a full recharge of a 2 kWh station). For faster in-vehicle charging, install a DC-to-DC charger like the Anker SOLIX Alternator Charger ($199) which accepts 30-50 A from the alternator, cutting recharge time to 4-6 hours of driving.
 Is gasoline generator + small power station better than just a bigger power station? 
 + For long-trip boondocking, yes. A [Honda EU2200i](/guides/honda-eu2200i-review-2026) or [Champion 8500W TRIFUEL](/reviews/champion-8500w-trifuel) generator + a 1,500 Wh power station provides indefinite power with a few gallons of fuel, vs a single large station that depletes after 1-2 days off-solar. The generator charges the station during quiet hours; the station provides silent power overnight. Combined cost is typically $1,200-$1,800 total vs $3,000+ for a single large unit.
 Bottom line
 For most RVers, the Bluetti AC200L is the right pick: built-in TT-30 outlet, 13.5K BTU AC startup, 1,200 W solar input, $999 street. For RVers who prioritize app monitoring and scheduling, the EcoFlow Delta 2 Max is the lateral move. For fifth-wheels and Class A motorhomes needing 50 A power, the Anker SOLIX F3800 is the only single-unit answer.
 For smaller setups (popups, tent trailers), the Bluetti AC180 covers essentials at $699 street. For quiet camping in shared sites, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the noise leader. For solar-first boondockers, the DJI Power 1000 V2 has the highest solar input ceiling in its class.
 Pair any of these with a soft-start kit on your rooftop AC for the best ROI upgrade — every dollar spent on a $350 soft-start saves $1,500 worth of generator capacity.
